To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) two downbursts from the same storm can cause severe damage; (ii) a storm with a high propagation speed may be sufficient for the occurrence of damaging downbursts even in the absence of a mesocyclone; and (iii) the storm's potential was well detected in advance.
the storm was characterized by a mesocyclone and that the two observed downbursts were most likely triggered by melting hail.
(i) a downburst-producing storm can be identified by a mesocyclone signature and (ii) the radar software CONRAD can provide a reliable forecast of downbursts and their potential for damage.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how a storm with a low probability of downburst activity can produce a multiple downburst event with severe damage.
the question of how the storm's dynamics, thermodynamics and microphysics were related to the downburst formation and propagation.
the identification of the physical causes of a multiple downburts, the verification of their occurrence and the analysis of their propagation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the storm's potential was correctly detected by CONRAD but that the downburst warning was not issued due to the storm's fast propagation.
the storm was not an ordinary downburst-producing event.
a downburst event is possible at any time of the year, even in the climatological annual minimum, if the synoptic conditions and the storm dynamics are favourable.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the downburst-producing storm was characterized by a combination of favorable environmental and mesoscale conditions.

the two downburst events were caused by a storm that had a rather typical convective structure and a rather atypical dynamic structure, and that the downbursts themselves had a rather typical thermodynamic structure.
the downburst events were not only caused by the strong winds, but also by the high storm motion. The latter, together with the lack of a warning, led to severe damage in the affected area.
The main takeaway from our work is that
even in the annual minimum of downbursts, the potential for damaging downbursts should not be underestimated.
the radar signature for a downburst-producing thunderstorm is not unique.

the combination of Doppler radar observations with ground lightning detection and aerial survey data is an effective tool for investigating downbursts, especially in regions where ground-based wind measurements are sparse.
